Huobi Founder Leon Li Sells London Mansion for £190M After Buying It for £139M

According to the Financial Times, Huobi founder Leon Li recently sold The Holme, a mansion in London's Regent's Park, for approximately £190 million. Li purchased the property for £139 million in 2024, resulting in a price difference of roughly £51 million in less than two years. Li's ownership had not previously been made public because the property was held through a UK subsidiary of trust services provider Zedra. The buyer was Abbas Sajwani, son of Dubai property developer Hussain Sajwani. — link

Robinhood Co-founder and CEO Vlad Tenev said that public companies should control the rights attached to their shares, but not every lawful use investors make of those shares after acquiring them. Binance Research said the tokenized stock market is shifting from an issuance race to a competition over distribution and usage. CoinShares: Latest CPI Print Not Particularly Helpful for Bitcoin

CoinShares said the latest CPI print was not particularly helpful for Bitcoin. Headline inflation was broadly in line with expectations, while core inflation came in slightly above forecasts, raising the probability of a September rate hike and the risk that monetary policy remains restrictive for longer. With no dovish catalyst from CPI, Bitcoin’s near-term upside is likely to remain constrained, and a move above $80,000 may require weaker economic data, a more dovish Fed, or another policy catalyst. — link

Latin America’s Largest Digital Bank Nu Launches in U.S. and Unveils USDC/EURC Global Account

Nu has launched operations in the U.S. while separately introducing Nu Global, a multi-currency digital account for cross-border users. Its U.S. offering includes deposit accounts, credit cards and international transfers through partner bank Lead Bank, while Nu Global converts deposits into USDC or EURC and supports transfers across more than 35 countries. Nu said it serves more than 140 million customers globally. — link

Canada Says Tokenized Deposits Are Legally the Same as Traditional Bank Deposits

Canada Says Tokenized Deposits Are Legally the Same as Traditional Bank Deposits Canada’s banking regulator OSFI said tokenized deposits are not legally distinct from traditional bank deposits, reinforcing a technology-neutral regulatory approach. The clarification means federally regulated banks can develop blockchain-based deposit products without requiring a separate regulatory category, while existing prudential, technology and risk-management rules continue to apply. — link
